text:
Course Learning Objectives
By the end of the semester, you will be able to…

analyze real-world data to answer questions about multivariable relationships.
use R to fit and evaluate linear and logistic regression models.
assess whether a proposed model is appropriate and describe its limitations.
use Quarto to write reproducible reports.
effectively communicate statistical results through writing and oral presentations.

The College of Idaho is committed to offering all students experiential learning opportunities and High-Impact Practices (HIP). In this specific course, students will participate in: collaborative assignments, research projects, simulations, testing original hypotheses, common experiences, public sharing of student generated material, and real world application of material as part of our college-wide, evidence-based approach to teaching and learning. These practices are designed to help students engage with the content, master core concepts, and understand how to apply skills in real world settings.

Lectures
Lectures are designed to be interactive, so you gain experience applying new concepts and learning from each other. My role as instructor is to introduce you to new methods, tools, and techniques, but it is up to you to take them and make use of them. A lot of what you do in this course will involve writing code, and coding is a skill that is best learned by doing. Therefore, as much as possible, you will be working on a variety of tasks and activities throughout each lecture and lab. You are expected to prepare for class by completing assigned readings, attend all lecture sessions, and meaningfully contribute to in-class exercises and discussion. Additionally, some lectures will feature application exercises that will be graded based on completing what we do in class.
You are expected to bring a laptop, tablet, or Chromebook to each class so that you can participate in the in-class exercises. Please make sure your device is fully charged before you come to class, as the number of outlets in the classroom may not be sufficient to accommodate everyone.

Activities & Assessment
You will be assessed based on four components: application exercises, homework, project, and written exams.

Application Exercises
Most lectures will have Application Exercises (AEs) that go along with them. These exercises will give you an opportunity to practice applying the statistical concepts and code introduced in the readings and lectures. Typically, students who are present will receive full credit on AEs for completion of the exercise. Students who are late to class or miss class entirely (without an excuse) will be graded for correctness.


Homework
In homework, you will apply what you’ve learned during lecture to complete data analysis tasks. You may discuss homework assignments with other students; however, homework should be completed and submitted individually.


Exams
There will be two in-class exams in this course. Each exam will be completed without a computer and will be closed notes. Through these exams you have the opportunity to demonstrate what you’ve learned in the course thus far. The exams will focus on conceptual understanding of the content. The content of the exam will be related to the content in reading assignments, lectures, application exercises, and homework assignments. More detail about the exams will be given during the semester.


Project
The purpose of the final project is to apply what you’ve learned throughout the semester to analyze an interesting data-driven research question. The project will be completed in groups of two, and each group will present their work through a written report and poster presentation taking place during the final exam. More information about the project will be provided during the semester.

text:
Five tips for success
Your success in this course depends very much on you and the effort you put into it. The course has been organized so that the burden of learning is on you. I will help you by providing you with materials and answering questions and setting a pace, but for this to work you must do the following:

Complete all the preparation work before class.
Ask questions. As often as you can. In class, out of class. Ask me, ask your friends, ask the person sitting next to you. This will help you more than anything else. If you get a question wrong on an assessment, ask why. If you’re not sure about the homework, ask. If you hear something on the news that sounds related to what we discussed, ask. If the reading is confusing, ask.
Do the readings.
Do the homework. The earlier you start, the better. It’s not enough to just mechanically plow through the exercises. You should ask yourself how these exercises relate to earlier material, and imagine how they might be changed (to make questions for an exam, for example.)
Don’t procrastinate. The content builds upon what was taught in previous weeks, so if something is confusing to you on Day 2, Day 3 will become more confusing, Day 4 even worse, etc. Don’t let the week end with unanswered questions. But if you find yourself falling behind and not knowing where to begin asking, come to office hours and I can help you identify a good (re)starting point.

Course policies

Academic honesty
TL;DR: Don’t cheat!

The homework assignments must be completed individually but you are welcome to discuss the assignment with classmates (e.g., discuss what’s the best way for approaching a problem, what functions are useful for accomplishing a particular task, etc.). However you may not directly share (i.e. via copy/paste or copying) answers to homework questions (including and especially any code) with anyone other than myself.
For the projects, collaboration within teams is not only allowed, but expected. Communication between teams at a high level is also allowed however you may not share code or components of the project across teams.


Reusing code
Unless explicitly stated otherwise, you may make use of online resources (e.g. StackOverflow) for coding examples on assignments. If you directly use code from an outside source (or use it as inspiration), you must explicitly cite where you obtained the code. Any recycled code that is discovered and is not explicitly cited will be treated as plagiarism. Furthermore, you are responsible for understanding the code you submit.


Coding conventions
Unless explicitly stated otherwise, you are expected to complete all assignments using only functions and packages introduced in class. If you would like to use a different set of tools, you must email Dr. Friedlander for permission. Any code that deviates from the conventions of the course will receive zero credit.


College of Idaho AI Statement
Artificial Intelligence (AI) policies and practices vary between professors, courses, and assignments. Some faculty members may encourage or even require the use of AI, while others will prohibit AI use. There is not a single approach that suits all subjects, so students need to be prepared to follow individual course AI policies. Navigating varying AI course policies prepares students for the real world where different workplaces, industries, and projects require situation-specific, adaptable, and ethical use of AI.


Dr. Friedlanders Thoughts on AI



Generative AI tools can assist in providing explanations and suggestions and can be very useful when used correctly. However, these tools should not be used for direct answers to graded assignments. You should not submit AI-generated content as your own work. I will be honest, AI can correctly complete many (if not most) of the problems that I will assign you in this class, and frankly, I believe that using LLMs will be an important skill for the workplace. However, it is not just the content of this course that is important. It is the process of learning, the ability to solve problems, the ability to craft and interpret quantitative arguments, and the growth that you experience because of, what education researchers call, productive struggle. Please remember that your skills and knowledge are the prodcut of this class not the work you complete in this class and the assignments you turn in. See the meme to the left for a humorous take on the situation.
This is a 2000-level course, meaning we are still providing you with the foundational knowledge necessary to succeed in more advanced courses. I will frequently be asking you to complete exercises without the use of AI, even though AI can complete them. The reason is that the skills and knowledge you gain from this course will (a) be built on in future courses and (b) allow you to extend beyond this material and get to a place where you exceed the capabilities of AI.


Official AI Policy For This Course
In general, I prefer that you don’t use any generative AI tools to produce material in this course (unless directed otherwise). However, you may use AI to write code under the following circumstances:

AI tools for code: If you get completely stuck on a problem, you may use AI to generate the code for you. However, you must explicitly write “I got stuck here and had to use AI” AND THEN make an appointment with me to get extra help.
No AI tools for narrative: Unless instructed otherwise, AI is not permitted for writing narrative on assignments. In general, you may use AI as a resource as you complete assignments but not to answer the exercises for you. You are ultimately responsible for the work you turn in; it should reflect your understanding of the course content.

If any uncited AI use is suspected, Dr. Friedlander reserves the right to invite you to a meeting in which you are asked to explain your answer. If you are unable to do so, you will receive a zero for the assignment, regardless of whether you used AI or not.
If you are unsure if the use of a particular resource complies with the academic honesty policy, please ask.
Regardless of course delivery format, it is the responsibility of all students to understand and follow all College of Idaho policies, including academic integrity (e.g., completing one’s own work, following proper citation of sources, adhering to guidance around group work projects, and more). Ignoring these requirements is a violation of the Honor Code.



Late work policy
The due dates for assignments are there to help you keep up with the course material and to ensure the teaching team can provide feedback within a timely manner. I understand that things come up periodically that could make it difficult to submit an assignment by the deadline.

Late Homework: There will be a 5% deduction for each 24-hour period the assignment is late for the first two days. After 2 days, students will receive a 30% reduction. No homework will be accepted after it is returned to the class

title: Residuals, Least Squares, and Model Evaluation
section: From Mean to Variability and SSE
text:
From Mean to Variability and SSE

But what is the best number we can use?
Can’t sum them because some are negative…
What if we square each of the residuals to make them positive and then sum them?

We’ll call this the Sum of Squared Error (SSE)
The mean gives use the smallest SSE possible for any single number

Why not just use the median?…

Historically: can be done with calculus
Luckily: has nice theoretical properties that go far beyond the scope of this class

Also… mean is the center… the SSE gives us a measure of how spread out our observations are… it gives us an idea of the amount of variation or variability in our data
Remember: the goals of statistics is to explain variability

title: Residuals, Least Squares, and Model Evaluation
text:
Least squares regression

We need a rule for picking the line, not just a line.
Least squares method: choose \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) to minimize the sum of squared error \[
\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - (\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i))^2
\]
If we use \(\bar{x}\) for our model this shoud look a little familiar \[
SST = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{x})^2
\]

This is the numerator in the calculation of variance/standard deviation
We can this of this as the Total Variation in our response variable

Basic idea: choose the line that explains the most variation in the data
How does one actually do this?…. Calculus (beyond the scope of this course)



Click here for details on deriving the equations for slope and intercept, which is easy if you know multivariate calculus.

title: Residuals, Least Squares, and Model Evaluation
text:
Let’s think about variation

DATA = MODEL + ERROR
\(\substack{\text{Total Variation} \\ \text{in Y}} = \substack{\text{Variation explained} \\ \text{by model}} + \substack{\text{Variation not explained} \\ \text{by model}}\)
\(SST = SSM + SSE\) (Note, you may see other acronym like \(SSR\) instead of \(SSE\))
\(SST\) = Sum of Squares Total (same as SSE if we use the mean as our model)
\(SSE\) = Sum of Squares Error (the amount of variation not explained by the model)
\(SSM\) = Sum of Squares Model (the amount of variation explained by the model)

We’ve calculated both the \(SST\) and \(SSE\)… we can get the SSM using subtraction: \(SST = SSM + SSE\)

Every point’s residual is a leftover piece of variation the model didn’t explain.

title: Residuals, Least Squares, and Model Evaluation
text:
Properties of least squares regression

Passes through the center of mass point, the coordinates corresponding to average \(X\) and average \(Y\): \(\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}\)
Slope has same sign as the correlation coefficient: \(\hat{\beta}_1 = r \frac{s_Y}{s_X}\)

\(r\): correlation coefficient
\(s_Y, s_X\): sample standard deviations of \(X\) and \(Y\)

Sum of the residuals is zero: \(\sum_{i = 1}^n e_i \approx 0\) (sound familiar?)

Intuition: Residuals are “balanced”

The residuals and \(X\) values are uncorrelated

title: Residuals, Least Squares, and Model Evaluation
text:
Partitioning Variability (ANOVA)

\(y_i - \bar{y} = (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}) + (y_i-\hat{y}_i)\)
Square and sum: \(\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2 = \sum(\hat{y} - \bar{y})^2 + \sum(y-\hat{y})^2\)
\(\substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{Total}} = \substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{model}} + \substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{error}}\)
\(SSTotal = SSModel + SSE\)
\(SST = SSM + SSE\)
This process of partitioning variability is called Analysis of Variance (ANOVA): Analysis of Variance
Involves a whole different way of thinking about modeling and experiemental design

\(R^2\): Percent Reduction in Error (PRE)

Our goal is to maximize the variation explained by our model (minimize the leftover error for our model)
It makes sense to ask… “How much has our model reduced the Total Error By”: \[
PRE = R^2 = \frac{SSM}{SST}
\]
We call this quantity the Precent Reduction in Error (PRE)…
More commonly it is simply referred to as \(R^2\)

Quantitative vs. categorical price

fit_cat: (Price as the explanatory variable) fits a separate mean for each of the 4 price levels — it has more “freedom” to match the data.
fit_num (PriceNum as the explanatory variable) forces those 4 means onto a single straight line.
Because a line is a special case of “4 free means,” fit_cat’s \(R^2\) can never be smaller than fit_num’s \(R^2\).
So why not always use the categorical version?

It can’t predict at a price it hasn’t seen, like $3.50.
It has no single “per dollar” slope to interpret or report.
It uses more parameters to explain (possibly) only a little more variation

title: Residuals, Least Squares, and Model Evaluation
text:
Recap

A residual is the leftover gap between an observed value and the model’s prediction: \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\).
The least squares method picks \(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1\) to minimize \(\sum e_i^2\).
Can decompose total variation (SST) into variation explained by the model (SSM) and leftover variation (SSE).
Two metrics for evaluating and comparing models:

\(R^2\): What proportion of the variation in the response variable is explained by the model?
\(RMSE\): How far does my model miss by, on average?

\(R^2\) depends on the data it was fit to, not just the true relationship — so it can’t be compared across data sets that vary different things.

title: HW 01: Dr. F’s Coffee
text:
Visualizing the data
We’ll start by taking a look at our response variable vibes_rating.

Remember the two questions you should ask before plotting a variable:

How many variables am I trying to visualize?
What type of variables are they?

Consider vibes_rating. Answer the two questions above, then specify what type(s) of plots would be most appropriate. (List at least two.)





In the code chunk that is in the answer block below, create at least one of the plots you specified above to visualize vibes_rating. Then use favstats to calculate summary statistics for vibes_rating.
Use the plot and summary statistics to describe the distribution of vibes_rating: comment on its shape, center, spread, and the presence of any apparent outliers.




Now let’s look at the categorical variables. The code below makes a bar chart of roast:

gf_bar(~roast, data = coffee) |>
  gf_labs(x = "Roast",
       y = "Count",
       title = "Distribution of Roast Levels")








Note that we haven’t talked about the symbol |> or the function gf_labs in class. The function gf_labs is used to add informative axis labels and a title to a ggplot object. The symbol |> is called a “pipe” operator and is used to chain together multiple functions in a readable way. When you encounter a pipe in code say “and then” to yourself in your head. For the code above you can say “Make a bar chart of roast and then add informative axis labels and a title.”

Using code for a bar chart as a template, create your own bar charts for origin and brewer, each with an informative title and axis labels. Note that some of the categories may overlap or be messy, don’t worry about fixing that yet.
Which roast, origin, and brewer show up most often in Dr. F’s coffee log? You’ll likely notice that some of the categories are messy and don’t appear in a nice order. We’ll talk about how to fix this later on. For now, call out 1-3 things that you’d like to fix if you knew how.





Now examine the distributions of the five flavor sub-scores: aroma, sweetness, acidity, body, and finish. For each one, create a histogram (with an informative title and axis labels) and calculate summary statistics with favstats.
Based on your plots and summary statistics: Which sub-score varies the most from cup to cup? (Hint: look at the standard deviation, sd, in the favstats output.)





Remember, our ultimate goal is to figure out what makes the best cup of coffee. That is, we want to understand what factors contribute to a high vibes_rating. Let’s compare vibes_rating across categories. We want to generate one plot of vibes_rating vs. roast.
Answer these two questions about the plot and then state what kinds of plots you could make:

How many variables are we trying to visualize at once?
What kind of variables are these?






Make at least one of the plots you described above to visualize vibes_rating vs. roast and another plot of vibes_rating vs. origin. For each pair, also calculate favstats(vibes_rating ~ roast, data = coffee) (and the equivalent for origin). Based on your plots and summary statistics, what kinds of roasts does Dr. F seem to prefer? What about origins? Be sure to reference the group sizes (n in the favstats output): how much should we trust a comparison built on a group with only two or three cups?





Now do the same comparison for brewer: a side-by-side boxplot of vibes_rating by brewer, plus the corresponding favstats.
Even if one brewer has a noticeably higher mean rating, explain why we can’t conclude that brewer causes better-tasting coffee.

For each one, create a plot of vibes_rating against that sub-score. While you don’t need to write the answers here, remember to ask the two questions above.
For each relationship, do your best to describe its direction and strength.
Bonus: You’ll notice that since everything is on a scale from 1 to 10, alot of the points are overlapping and it’s hard to see the real relationships if you use gf_point. Instead try using gf_jitter. What do you think this does?

Starbucks often displays the total calories in their food items but not the other nutritional information. Carbohydrates are a body’s main fuel source. The Dietary Guidelines for America recommend that carbohydrates make up 45% to 65% of total daily calories. Our goal is to understand the relationship between the amount of carbohydrates and calories in Starbucks food items. We’d also like to assess if the relationship differs based on the type of food item (bakery, salad, sandwich, etc.)
You will now be introduced to the functions we will use most frequently for exploratory data analysis (EDA) in this class. The first part of this document contains explanations for beginning R users, but all students should work through the entire document.

title: AE 02: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Loading Packages
R is an open source programming language and environment for statistical computing and graphics. This means that anyone can use R for free, and anyone can contribute to the development of R. R has a large ecosystem of packages that extend its functionality. You can think of these like expansion packs for R. If you’re on your own computer, each packages needs to be install once using the function install.packages(). Since we’re working in the cloud, we don’t need to do this step. Regardless of what computer you’re on each package needs to be loaded using the function library() every timne you want to use it We typically load all packages at the beginning of our scripts and Quarto files.

The code below loads the package called tidyverse which provides many functions that will be useful for manipulating data and the package called mosaic which is useful for teaching statistics. Add another line that loads a package called ggformula which we will use to plot our data and a third that loads the package openintro which will contain our data for this activity. function( Y ~ X, data = DataSetName )

function is an R function that dictates something you want to do with your data; for example,

Useful code for cleaning data (requires dplyr, loaded via library(tidyverse))
These examples use dcbikeshare (columns like season, count, temp_orig, hour) as a running example, so column names below are real rather than generic placeholders.

Keep only rows matching a condition: dcbikeshare |> filter(season == "fall")

dcbikeshare |>

  summarize(avg_count = mean(count), median_count = median(count))
if_else: recode a column into two categories
dcbikeshare |>

  mutate(season = case_when(
    season == 1 ~ "winter",
    season == 2 ~ "spring",
    season == 3 ~ "summer",
    season == 4 ~ "fall"

  mutate(season = factor(season, levels = c("winter", "spring", "summer", "fall")))

title: Project 2: Power Analysis
text:
Explanation of Power Analysis
A power analysis estimates the sample size required to detect an effect of a given size with a given degree of confidence. In this assignment, you will use the pilot data collected in Part 1 to estimate the sample size needed to detect the effect you are interested in studying.
The power of a statistical test is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative hypothesis is true. To calculate this number, we need to assume something called an effect size. The effect size is a measure of the magnitude of the effect of the treatment or intervention being studied. Larger effect sizes are easier to detect, while smaller effect sizes require larger sample sizes to achieve the same level of power.
Power is affected by several factors, including:

Effect size: Larger effects are easier to detect, requiring smaller sample sizes.
Sample size: Larger samples provide more information and increase power.
Significance level (()): Lowering () (e.g., from 0.05 to 0.01) reduces power.
Variability: More variable data requires larger samples to detect effects.

Loading Data From A File

PATH: directions to get to a file

Example: “ae/ae-03/dataset.csv” will take it you to ae then ae-03 then dataset.csv

Two types of paths: absolute and relative

Absolute: starts from the root directory (i.e. the top-level directory)
Relative: starts from the current directory (.. goes up one level)

RStudio & Quarto: use read_csv("relative_path/to/file.csv") to load data from a CSV file

Brief aside: one of the few things we put in quotes in R. Use quotes when:

You want R to look outside of R for something
You are defining a string (i.e. a “word” in R)

dplyr and the tidyverse

As R is an open-source programming language there are several difference styles and ways of doing things
In this class we’re going to use something called the tidyverse
The tidyverse is a collection of R packages that share a common design philosophy
dplyr is a package within the tidyverse that provides a consistent interface for data manipulation

title: Cleaning Our Data
text:
dplyr verbs

dplyr provides a set of “verbs” for data manipulation
We’ll going to cover two today:

mutate: creates new columns and changes (mutates) existing columns
filter: selects rows based on a condition

Your HW will go over two more:

summarize: compute summary statistics (e.g. mean, median, standard deviation)
group_by: group data by one or more variables (use this before summarize usually)

We’ll typically chain together these verbs using the pipe operator |> (you may see %>% in older code)
Let’s use these verbs to clean up the bikeshare data

Data prep

R calls categorical data “factors”

You may also see <chr> which stands for character. These are also categorical variables, but it’s almost always better to convert them to factors

Factors remember what all possible levels (categories) and store them in order

You can put them in an order that makes sense so your plots looks better

Idea:

Take the bikeshare data… AND THEN

Solution

bikeshare <- bikeshare |>
  mutate(season = case_when(
    season == 1 ~ "winter",
    season == 2 ~ "spring",
    season == 3 ~ "summer",
    season == 4 ~ "fall"
  ),
  season = factor(season, levels = c("winter", "spring", "summer", "fall")))

Indicator variables

Suppose a categorical variable has \(K\) categories (levels).
We can make \(K\) indicator variables, one per category.
An indicator variable takes the value 1 or 0:

1 if the observation belongs to that category
0 if it does not

Finally… we drop one of the indicator variables.
This category is called the reference level (or baseline) and it doesn’t get its own term in the model

title: Categorical Predictors
text:
Indicators in the model

We only use \(K - 1\) of the indicator variables in the model.
The reference level (or baseline) is the category left out — it doesn’t get its own term.
The coefficient on each indicator is the expected difference in the response compared to the baseline.
This is called dummy coding, and R does it for you.

R’s default reference level
By default, R picks the reference level either alphabetically (if variable is not a factor) or the first level (if variable is a factor).
Most of the time, you probably don’t care which level is chosen to be the reference level (you need to know which one it is though)… but if you do chage it using the same trick from season in Lecture 3:

Intercept: we predict a winter (baseline) day to have \(\hat\beta_0\) rentals, on average — this is the winter mean.

title: Categorical Predictors
text:
Recap


Regression works with a categorical predictor \(X\), just like a quantitative one.
R recodes a \(K\)-level categorical variable into \(K - 1\) indicator (dummy) variables.
The left-out category is the reference level; by default R picks it alphabetically, but we can set it with factor(x, levels = ...).
The intercept is the mean of the response at the reference level.
Each slope is the difference in means between that level and the reference level.
Correlation doesn’t apply to categorical predictors, but regression still does.
